note: New York has something most states do not: the Justice Center for the Protection of People with Special Needs, created by statute in 2013, with its own 24-hour register, its own investigators and the power to support criminal prosecution. It says every allegation is investigated to conclusion, and it provides advocates to victims and families during the investigation. If the program is a New York state-operated, licensed or certified facility, this is the strongest channel in the state.

civil_injury.summary: One year for intentional harm: assault, battery and false imprisonment. Three years for negligence (for example, a program's negligent supervision or hiring). If the person who hurt you is criminally prosecuted, you get at least one year after the criminal case ends to sue them.
civil_injury.citation: N.Y. C.P.L.R. 215(3) (intentional torts, 1 year); 214(5) (personal injury/negligence, 3 years); 215(8)(a) (criminal-action extension)
civil_injury.quote: The following actions shall be commenced within one year: ... 3. an action to recover damages for assault, battery, false imprisonment, malicious prosecution, libel, slander, false words causing special damages, or a violation of the right of privacy
civil_injury.note: CPLR 214(5) (https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/CVP/214): 'an action to recover damages for a personal injury except as provided in sections 214-b, 214-c, 214-i and 215' - three years. 215(8)(a): where a criminal action is commenced against the same defendant for the same event, the plaintiff has 'at least one year from the termination of the criminal action'. 215(9): injury from domestic violence has two years (not usually relevant to programs). Child sexual abuse claims have separate rules (CPLR 208(b), 214-g), not covered here.

civil_minor_tolling.summary: Yes. For a one-year claim (assault, battery), the time you were under 18 is not counted, so the deadline is your 19th birthday. For a three-year negligence claim, you have three years after turning 18 (your 21st birthday). The 10-year cap in this statute does not apply to minors except in medical malpractice. No general extended period for physical (non-sexual) child abuse.
civil_minor_tolling.quote: the time within which the action must be commenced shall be extended to three years after the disability ceases ... if the time otherwise limited is less than three years, the time shall be extended by the period of disability.
civil_minor_tolling.note: Same subsection: 'shall not be extended by this provision beyond ten years after the cause of action accrues, except, in any action other than for medical, dental or podiatric malpractice, where the person was under a disability due to infancy.' So the 10-year cap does NOT limit a minor's assault or negligence claim (the task brief's example of a '10-year infancy toll cap' applies only to malpractice or to insanity). Infancy for CPLR purposes means under 18 (CPLR 105(j); definition not re-read for this research).

civil_government_claims.summary: Against a county, city, town, village or school district: serve a notice of claim within 90 days and sue within one year and 90 days. Against New York State (Court of Claims): file the claim, or a notice of intention to file, within 90 days; then the claim is due within two years for negligence or one year for intentional torts. Minors get extra time under the tolling rules.
civil_government_claims.quote: (c) the action or special proceeding shall be commenced within one year and ninety days after the happening of the event upon which the claim is based
civil_government_claims.note: 50-e(1)(a) (https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GMU/50-E, revision of 2026-02-20): notice of claim 'within ninety days after the claim arises'; courts may allow late notice under 50-e(5). Court of Claims Act 10(3) negligence: 90 days, or notice of intention then 'within two years after the accrual'; 10(3-b) intentional torts: 90 days, or notice of intention then 'within one year after the accrual'; 10(5): 'If the claimant shall be under legal disability, the claim may be presented within two years after such disability is removed.' (https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/CTC/10). CPLR 208 infancy tolling applies to the 50-i period, but the interaction with the 90-day notice (late-notice motion) is fact-specific; confidence medium for that reason. 'years' is 1.25 for the 1 year 90 days local-government period.

criminal_child_abuse.summary: Five years from the offense for felony physical abuse of a child (charged as felony assault). Endangering the welfare of a child is a misdemeanor: two years. The clock does not pause until the child is older for physical abuse; the age-23 rule applies only to sexual offenses, incest and child sexual performance.
criminal_child_abuse.quote: (b) A prosecution for any other felony must be commenced within five years after the commission thereof; (c) A prosecution for a misdemeanor must be commenced within two years after the commission thereof
criminal_child_abuse.note: New York has no stand-alone felony 'child abuse' crime; physical abuse is charged as assault (Penal Law 120.05, 120.10) or similar, and endangering the welfare of a child (Penal Law 260.10) is a class A misdemeanor. 30.10(3)(f) delays the start to age 23 (or report) only for 'a sexual offense as defined in article one hundred thirty' and related incest/sexual performance crimes. Time the defendant is continuously out of state or whereabouts unknown is excluded, up to five extra years (30.10(4)(a)). Class A felonies have no limit (30.10(2)(a)).

criminal_felony_assault.summary: Five years from the offense for felony assault (first- or second-degree). Misdemeanor (third-degree) assault: two years.
criminal_felony_assault.quote: (b) A prosecution for any other felony must be commenced within five years after the commission thereof; (c) A prosecution for a misdemeanor must be commenced within two years after the commission thereof
criminal_felony_assault.note: Current text is the 2024-07-26 revision on nysenate.gov. Class A felonies (e.g., some assault-related homicide-level offenses) may be commenced at any time.

channels.name: New York Office of the Professions, Office of Professional Discipline
channels.what_it_can_do: Investigates professional misconduct by anyone licensed by the State of New York - psychologists, mental health counselors, marriage and family therapists, creative arts therapists, psychoanalysts and social workers - and illegal practice by the unlicensed. Outcomes run from a warning letter to revoking the licence.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed mental health professional in New York, or someone practising without the licence.
channels.how: Complete the discipline complaint form and post it to the regional Office of Professional Discipline nearest where the incident happened, or fax it. Complaints must be in writing; they cannot be made by phone, though you can call for help with the form.
channels.phone_note: For information on filing. The complaint itself has to be in writing. Fax 212-951-6420.
channels.note: Investigators in the regional office may consult members of the State board for that profession before deciding.

channels.name: New York State Justice Center for the Protection of People with Special Needs
channels.what_it_can_do: Runs the Vulnerable Persons Central Register, a 24-hour hotline for abuse, neglect, financial misappropriation and any significant incident threatening the health, safety or welfare of someone in a New York state-operated, licensed or certified facility. It investigates every allegation to conclusion, and works with prosecutors on criminal cases arising from them.
channels.who_to_report: A young person with special needs - which includes a mental health diagnosis - receiving services at a New York state-operated, licensed or certified facility or program.
channels.how: Call the Vulnerable Persons Central Register. If somebody is in immediate danger, call 911 first.
channels.phone_note: Vulnerable Persons Central Register, 24 hours a day. Advocates for victims and families on 1-800-624-4143.
channels.note: The Justice Center provides advocates who answer questions about the process and give case updates during an investigation - unusual, and worth using.

channels.name: New York Statewide Central Register of Child Abuse and Maltreatment
channels.what_it_can_do: The state's child abuse hotline, run by the Office of Children and Family Services. Takes reports from the general public and routes them to the local child protective service for investigation.
channels.who_to_report: A child at a New York program. Neighbours, relatives and concerned citizens can all use the public line.
channels.how: Call the 24-hour toll-free line. If a child is in immediate danger, call 911 or the local police first.
channels.phone_note: 24 hours a day. TDD/TTY 1-800-638-5163, or have a Video Relay provider call the main number.

channels.name: Disability Rights New York
channels.what_it_can_do: New York's Protection and Advocacy agency, with federal authority to investigate abuse and neglect of people with disabilities in facilities, a right of access to them, and free legal advocacy.
channels.who_to_report: A New York program where the young person has a disability or a mental health diagnosis.

channels.name: New York OCFS and OMH residential facility oversight
channels.what_it_can_do: The Office of Mental Health regulates residential treatment facilities for children and youth, and the OCFS Regional Office investigates child abuse and neglect allegations involving facilities OMH licenses or operates. Between them they hold the licence and investigate what happens inside it.
channels.who_to_report: A New York residential treatment facility - unsafe conditions, inadequate supervision, hygiene and health neglect, anything that is a standards failure rather than one person's conduct.
channels.how: Report through the OCFS portal or the Statewide Central Register. For a licensed facility the Justice Center's Vulnerable Persons Central Register is usually the stronger route.
channels.phone_note: Statewide Central Register line used for reports about facilities.
